concept.overview: Observability is the ability to understand what a system is doing from the outside using its telemetry: metrics, logs, and traces. Prometheus is a time-series database and monitoring system that scrapes numeric metrics from your applications and infrastructure, stores them, and evaluates alerting rules. Grafana is the visualization layer that turns those metrics into dashboards and graphs. Together with a logging stack (like Loki or the ELK stack), they let you see trends, spot anomalies, and get paged before users notice an outage.
concept.whyItMatters: You cannot operate what you cannot see. Monitoring turns a black-box production system into something you can reason about: is latency rising, is the error rate spiking, is the disk about to fill? Good observability shortens the time to detect and resolve incidents, validates that deployments are healthy, and provides the data behind SLOs and capacity planning. It is the feedback loop that makes reliable operations possible.
useCases: Tracking golden signals — latency, traffic, errors, saturation — per service
Alerting on-call engineers when thresholds or SLOs are breached
Visualizing system and application health on shared dashboards
Correlating a deploy with a change in error rate or latency
Aggregating and searching logs to debug incidents quickly
concept.architecture: Applications expose metrics on an HTTP /metrics endpoint in the Prometheus text format, often via a client library or an exporter (node_exporter for hosts, cAdvisor for containers). Prometheus periodically scrapes these targets (discovered statically or via service discovery), stores the samples in its time-series database, and evaluates recording and alerting rules written in PromQL. When an alert fires, it is sent to Alertmanager, which deduplicates, groups, and routes notifications to Slack, PagerDuty, or email. Grafana queries Prometheus (and other data sources) with PromQL to render dashboards. Logs flow through a separate pipeline (Fluent Bit/Promtail -> Loki/Elasticsearch) and can be correlated with metrics in Grafana.

bestPractices: Alert on symptoms users feel (error rate, latency), not just causes (CPU), to reduce noise.
Base alerts on SLOs and burn rates so paging is meaningful and actionable.
Use labels thoughtfully; high-cardinality labels (user IDs) explode storage.
Make every alert actionable and linked to a runbook; delete alerts nobody acts on.
Keep dashboards focused on the golden signals per service, not vanity metrics.
pitfalls: Alert fatigue from too many noisy, non-actionable alerts — real ones get ignored.
High-cardinality labels blowing up Prometheus memory and storage.
Alerting only on CPU/memory while users experience errors you never see.
Dashboards full of graphs no one understands or acts on.
No Alertmanager grouping, so one incident produces hundreds of pages.
cheatSheet: RED method: Rate, Errors, Duration per request
USE method: Utilization, Saturation, Errors per resource

quiz.question: How does Prometheus collect metrics from targets?
quiz.explanation: Prometheus uses a pull model, scraping HTTP /metrics endpoints on an interval.

quiz.question: What is Grafana primarily used for?
quiz.explanation: Grafana is the visualization layer; Prometheus stores and queries the data.

quiz.question: The four golden signals are latency, traffic, errors, and saturation.
quiz.explanation: These four indicators summarize user-facing service health.

quiz.question: Which component routes and deduplicates alerts?
quiz.explanation: Alertmanager groups, deduplicates, silences, and routes alerts to receivers.

quiz.question: You are paged constantly for brief CPU spikes that don't affect users. Best fix?
options: Alert on user-facing symptoms (error rate/latency/SLO) instead of raw CPU
quiz.explanation: Symptom-based, SLO-driven alerting reduces noise and pages only on real impact.

quiz.question: What does 'rate(http_requests_total[5m])' compute?
options: Per-second request rate over a 5-minute window
quiz.explanation: rate() gives the per-second average increase of a counter over the range.

quiz.question: High-cardinality labels like unique user IDs can overwhelm Prometheus.
quiz.explanation: Each label combination is a separate series; unbounded cardinality explodes memory/storage.

quiz.question: What is an exporter?
options: A component that exposes a system's metrics in Prometheus format
quiz.explanation: Exporters (e.g., node_exporter) translate system metrics into the scrape format.

quiz.question: Which PromQL finds targets that are down?
quiz.explanation: The 'up' metric is 1 when a scrape succeeds; up == 0 means the target is down.

quiz.question: After a deploy, error rate jumps. How do dashboards help confirm causation?
options: Overlay the deploy time with the error-rate graph to correlate
quiz.explanation: Correlating the deploy annotation with the metric change points to the deploy as the cause.

quiz.question: Every alert should be actionable and ideally linked to a runbook.
quiz.explanation: Non-actionable alerts cause fatigue; actionable alerts with runbooks speed resolution.

quiz.question: The RED method tracks which three per request?
quiz.explanation: RED = Rate, Errors, Duration — a request-focused monitoring method.

quiz.question: You want to page only when an SLO is truly at risk, not on every blip. Which approach?
options: Multi-window burn-rate alerting against the error budget
quiz.explanation: Burn-rate alerting on the error budget pages proportionally to real SLO risk.

tasks.title: Expose and scrape metrics
steps: Run node_exporter or an app exposing /metrics
Add a scrape_config for the target
Confirm the target is UP in the Prometheus UI
successCriteria: Metrics are queryable in the expression browser

tasks.title: Build a Grafana dashboard
steps: Add Prometheus as a Grafana data source
Create panels for request rate and error rate using PromQL
Add a p95 latency panel from a histogram
Save the dashboard and set a time range
successCriteria: Dashboard renders live data from Prometheus
Panels show rate, errors, and latency

tasks.title: Write an alerting rule
steps: Write a PromQL alert for high error rate over 5m
Add an Alertmanager route to a receiver (e.g., a webhook)
Trigger the condition and observe the alert fire
Add a runbook link to the alert annotations
successCriteria: The alert fires and routes to the receiver
The alert includes an actionable runbook link

tasks.title: Run an observability incident
tasks.goal: Detect and diagnose a simulated outage.
steps: Deploy a change that increases latency/errors
Watch the dashboard and let the alert fire
Use metrics and logs to localize the failing component
Roll back and confirm recovery on the dashboard
successCriteria: The alert detected the issue before manual discovery
